subject: ela
intro: These hard items ask you to read a full short narrative or multi-paragraph excerpt closely, then evaluate how the writer's techniques work together across the whole piece. You will judge openings, conclusions, pacing, coherence, transitions, and sequence in light of the story's context, narrator, and theme. Write your answer and a short justification for each.

items.prompt:
Read this short narrative.

"The lighthouse had been dark for three winters. Nobody in our town remembered how to light it, and the freighters now passed far out, where the rocks could not catch them. One October night, old Mr. Pell knocked on our door, soaked to the bone, and said a boat was lost in the fog. My father grabbed his coat. I followed him up the spiral stairs, counting each step in the dark. At the top, my father struck a match, and the great lamp shuddered, sputtered, and finally blazed. Far below, a horn answered."

Which ending best follows from and reflects on this narrative: (1) "Then we walked home and ate dinner. The end." or (2) "We never learned the name of the boat we saved, but for the rest of that winter the lamp burned every night, and I understood that some things are worth remembering how to do."? Explain your choice.
items.answer: Ending 2, because it grows out of the rescue and the lighthouse's dark history and reflects on the meaning of keeping the light alive, while ending 1 simply stops the action without connecting to the story.

steps: Identify the story's arc: a long-dark lighthouse is relit to save a lost boat in the fog.
A strong conclusion should follow from those events and reflect on what they meant.
Ending 1 only reports leaving and eating; it ignores the lighthouse, the rescue, and the narrator's feelings.
Ending 2 returns to the central image (the lamp), notes the lasting change (it burns every night), and offers reflection (some things are worth remembering how to do).
Choose ending 2 because it ties together context, narrator, and theme.

items.prompt:
Read this excerpt.

"Dad said the trail was easy. We started after lunch. The sun went down fast. We had no flashlight. I had wanted to bring one. We got lost near the creek. A ranger found us at midnight. We had left the house that morning excited."

This paragraph has one sentence that breaks the natural time sequence and hurts the story's flow. Which sentence is out of place, and where should the idea go instead?
items.answer: The sentence "We had left the house that morning excited" is out of place at the end. It describes the earliest moment in the story, so it belongs near the beginning, before "We started after lunch."

steps: List the events in the order the time line actually happened: leaving the house in the morning, starting after lunch, the sun setting, getting lost, the ranger finding them at midnight.
Scan the paragraph for a sentence whose time does not match its position.
The final sentence refers to that morning, the earliest point, yet it sits after the midnight rescue.
Moving it to the opening restores a natural beginning-to-end sequence.
Answer: relocate the last sentence to the start of the paragraph.

items.prompt:
Read this narrative opening.

"This is a story about the day my dog ran away. It was a sad day. My dog is named Biscuit. He is brown. I felt bad when he ran away. That is what this story is about."

The writer wants an opening that engages and orients the reader instead of flatly announcing the topic. Choose the stronger revision and explain why: (A) "This story is going to tell you all about when Biscuit, my brown dog, ran away and made me sad." or (B) "The gate stood open and the yard was empty. I called Biscuit's name until my voice cracked, but only the wind moved through the grass."
items.answer: Revision B, because it drops the flat announcement and instead establishes a scene (the open gate, the empty yard), introduces the narrator's situation, and uses sensory detail and action to draw the reader in. Revision A still just states the topic.

steps: A strong opening orients the reader to context and narrator and engages with detail rather than announcing the topic.
Revision A keeps the telling frame ("This story is going to tell you all about"), so it stays flat.
Revision B opens inside the action with concrete images (open gate, empty yard, cracking voice, wind in the grass).
Those details establish setting and feeling without naming them outright.
Choose B.

items.prompt:
Read this paragraph from the middle of a story.

"The bell rang for the final round of the spelling bee. My hands were sweating. The judge read my word. I spelled it letter by letter. I sat down. I won the trophy. My parents cheered."

The writer rushes through the most important moment with the same quick pacing used for minor details. Which single revision best slows the pacing to develop the key moment? (A) Add more about the bell ringing at the start. (B) Expand "I spelled it letter by letter" into a slower, detailed moment, such as "I closed my eyes, pictured the word on the page, and forced out each letter, pausing after every one as the gym held its breath." (C) Add a sentence about what the trophy looked like. Explain your choice.
items.answer: Revision B, because the climax of the story is the narrator spelling the winning word, and slowing that exact moment with description and the crowd's reaction gives it the weight it deserves. Options A and C expand minor details instead.

steps: Find the key moment of the paragraph: the narrator spelling the final word that wins the bee.
Good pacing slows down for key moments and speeds through minor ones.
Option A expands the bell (a minor setup detail); option C expands the trophy (an aftermath detail).
Option B stretches the actual spelling into a tense, detailed beat with sensory and crowd detail.
Choose B because it slows the climax, not a minor moment.

items.prompt:
Read this two-paragraph excerpt.

"All summer, Nadia had practiced the dive alone, climbing the high board after the pool closed and dropping into the dark water again and again. She told no one. ____ the day of the meet arrived, and she stood on the board with the whole town watching below."

Choose the transition that best fills the blank to signal the shift from the summer of secret practice to the day of the meet, and explain why: (A) "For example," (B) "In the same way," (C) "At last," (D) "Meanwhile,".
items.answer: C) "At last," because it signals the passage of time from the long summer of practice to the awaited day of the meet, marking the shift to a new moment. "For example" and "In the same way" show comparison, and "Meanwhile" suggests two things happening at once, which does not fit.

steps: Identify the relationship: the text moves from a whole summer of secret practice to the single day of the meet, a shift forward in time.
"For example" introduces an illustration, which is wrong here.
"In the same way" signals comparison, not a time shift.
"Meanwhile" means at the same time, but the meet comes after the summer.
"At last" conveys that the awaited moment has finally arrived, fitting the time shift; choose C.

items.prompt:
Read this short narrative.

"Grandpa handed me the old fishing rod the morning before he went into the hospital. 'This caught more dinners than I can count,' he said. That summer I took it to the lake almost every day, but I never caught a thing. People said I should buy a better rod. I kept using his."

Which conclusion best follows from and reflects on this narrative, and why? (A) "In August, I finally bought a brand new rod and caught a fish on the first cast." (B) "I never did catch much with that rod, but every time I cast it into the still water, it felt like Grandpa was standing beside me again, and that was the real catch." (C) "Fishing is a fun hobby that many people enjoy in the summer."
items.answer: Conclusion B, because it follows from the narrator's choice to keep using Grandpa's rod despite catching nothing and reflects on what the rod truly meant. Conclusion A contradicts that choice, and C is a generic statement unconnected to the story.

steps: Identify the story's heart: the narrator keeps a grandfather's rod, catching nothing, but treasuring the connection.
Conclusion A abandons the rod and contradicts the narrator's loyalty, undercutting the theme.
Conclusion C is a general comment about fishing, disconnected from these characters and events.
Conclusion B honors the choice to keep the rod and reflects that the value was the memory of Grandpa, not the fish.
Choose B.

items.prompt:
Read this paragraph.

"The storm hit at night. The food was really very extremely good at the shelter. Wind tore shingles off the roof. We huddled in the hallway with flashlights. Branches cracked outside like gunshots. My little sister gripped my hand."

One sentence both interrupts the tense mood and uses vague, padded wording instead of precise sensory detail. Identify that sentence and rewrite it so it either fits the mood with concrete detail or is removed.
items.answer: The sentence "The food was really very extremely good at the shelter" is the problem. It breaks the storm's tense mood and piles up vague intensifiers. It should be removed, or if food matters, replaced with a concrete detail that fits the scene, such as "Someone passed out crackers and warm cocoa that steamed in the dark."

steps: Note the paragraph's tense, sensory mood: wind, cracking branches, flashlights, a frightened sister.
Locate the sentence that clashes: the line about the food interrupts the tension.
Note its weak wording: "really very extremely good" stacks intensifiers instead of giving concrete detail.
Decide to cut it or replace it with specific sensory detail that fits the mood.
Provide a concrete replacement (steaming cocoa and crackers) or recommend removal.

items.prompt:
Read this narrative.

"On the last day of camp, I finally worked up the nerve to talk to the girl who always sat alone by the lake. I had watched her sketch for two weeks. My heart pounded as I walked over."

The writer wants to develop the next moment with dialogue that advances the action and reveals character, using correct punctuation. Choose the strongest option and explain why: (A) I felt nervous and shy as I came closer to her. (B) "Those are really good," I blurted, pointing at her sketchbook. "Could you teach me sometime?" (C) She said hi. (D) "Hi how are you the weather is nice today," I said quickly.
items.answer: B, because the spoken lines reveal the narrator's eagerness and shyness, advance the action by opening a real conversation, and are correctly punctuated. A only tells the feeling, C is flat and undeveloped, and D is off-topic and mispunctuated.

steps: The goal is dialogue that develops character and advances the action with correct punctuation.
Option A tells the emotion instead of showing it through speech.
Option C is vague and reveals nothing.
Option D is off-topic small talk and lacks proper comma punctuation inside the quotation.
Option B shows character through specific, in-scene speech and is correctly punctuated; choose B.

items.prompt:
Read these five events from a story, listed out of order.

(1) Mei opened her acceptance letter and screamed with joy.
(2) Mei spent the winter rehearsing her audition piece every night.
(3) Mei mailed her application to the music conservatory.
(4) Mei played her audition for the panel of judges.
(5) Mei first heard about the conservatory from her violin teacher.

Put the events in the order that unfolds naturally from beginning to end, and explain the cause-and-effect chain.
items.answer: Order: 5, 3, 2, 4, 1. Mei first hears about the conservatory, then mails her application, then rehearses through the winter, then plays the audition, and finally opens the acceptance letter. Each step causes or leads to the next.

steps: Find the earliest event: Mei hears about the conservatory from her teacher (5).
She must apply before she can audition, so she mails her application next (3).
She rehearses over the winter in preparation (2).
She plays the audition for the judges (4).
Last, she receives and opens the acceptance letter (1). Final order: 5, 3, 2, 4, 1.

items.prompt:
Read this excerpt.

"The new kid, Theo, never spoke in class. I figured he was stuck up. Then one rainy Tuesday I saw him crouched behind the gym, feeding a stray kitten from his own lunch. He looked up, embarrassed, and finally said something to me."

The writer wants a line of dialogue for Theo that develops his character and shifts the narrator's first impression. Choose the strongest option and justify it: (A) "What are you looking at?" (B) "Please don't tell anyone. She's too little to make it through the cold alone." (C) "Hi." (D) "I don't like you."
items.answer: B, because the line reveals Theo as quietly caring and worried about the kitten, which overturns the narrator's earlier judgment that he was stuck up, and it advances the relationship between the two characters. The other options are flat or contradict the gentle scene.

steps: Identify the purpose: dialogue that develops Theo and changes the narrator's impression of him as stuck up.
Option A is hostile and reinforces, not shifts, the bad first impression.
Option C is too flat to reveal character.
Option D contradicts the tender moment of feeding the kitten.
Option B shows Theo's protectiveness and vulnerability, reversing the narrator's judgment; choose B.

items.prompt:
Read this paragraph.

"We reached the summit at dawn. The view was nice. There were things to see all around us. It looked pretty good up there. We felt happy about it."

This paragraph relies on vague, flat wording. Rewrite it using precise words and sensory language (sight, sound, touch) to convey the experience vividly, keeping it to two or three sentences.
items.answer: A strong rewrite uses concrete sensory detail, for example: "We reached the summit just as the first light spilled over the ridge, turning the snow a soft pink. Far below, the valley lay wrapped in mist, silent except for the wind hissing across the rocks. The cold air stung my cheeks, but I could not stop grinning." This replaces "nice," "things," "pretty good," and "happy" with specific sights, sounds, and touch.

steps: Locate the vague words: "nice," "things to see," "pretty good," "felt happy."
Replace each with concrete, specific detail and sensory language.
Add sight (pink snow, misty valley), sound (wind hissing), and touch (cold air stinging).
Show the feeling through the grin rather than naming "happy."
Keep the rewrite to two or three vivid sentences.

items.prompt:
Read this short narrative.

"For weeks, Diego had told everyone he wasn't scared of the haunted corn maze. The night of the festival, his friends dared him to go in alone. He stepped between the tall stalks, the leaves whispering on every side, and the lantern light shrinking behind him. Something rustled. He froze."

Which ending best ties together the established setup (Diego's boasting) and the narrated experience, and reflects on it? (A) "It was just a rabbit. Diego laughed out loud, and when he came out the other side, he admitted to his friends that maybe he had been a little scared after all." (B) "Diego liked corn on the cob. The end." (C) "Suddenly a dragon appeared and Diego flew home on its back." Explain your choice.
items.answer: A, because it resolves the suspense (a harmless rabbit), connects to Diego's earlier boasting by having him honestly admit his fear, and reflects on the experience. B is unconnected and abrupt, and C breaks the realistic world of the story.

steps: Recall the setup: Diego boasted he was not scared, then froze at a rustling sound.
A fitting ending should resolve the moment and reflect on his earlier claim.
Option B is random and ignores the maze and his boasting.
Option C introduces a dragon, breaking the realistic narrative.
Option A reveals the harmless cause and circles back to his boast with an honest admission; choose A.

items.prompt:
Read this excerpt with two paragraphs.

"For three years, the community garden behind our building had been my grandmother's whole world. She knew every tomato plant by name and traded zucchini with the neighbors all summer.

____ the construction notice went up on the fence, and the bulldozers were scheduled for spring. My grandmother read the sign twice, folded her gloves, and said nothing."

Choose the transition that best opens the second paragraph to signal the shift in time and situation, and explain your reasoning: (A) "For instance," (B) "Then, one cold morning," (C) "Similarly," (D) "In conclusion,".
items.answer: B) "Then, one cold morning," because it signals the move from years of tending the garden to the specific later morning when the construction notice appears, marking a clear shift in time and situation. "For instance" and "Similarly" show illustration or comparison, and "In conclusion" signals an ending, none of which fit.

steps: Identify the relationship: a shift from three years of gardening to a particular later morning when bad news arrives.
"For instance" introduces an example, which is wrong.
"Similarly" signals comparison, not a time shift.
"In conclusion" wrongly signals the end of a piece.
"Then, one cold morning" marks the move forward in time to a new moment; choose B.

items.prompt:
Read this narrative excerpt.

"I had never beaten my older brother at chess. He'd taught me the game when I was six and won every match for years. On Sunday we played again. Move by move, I saw a trap forming, and for the first time he was the one who looked worried. When I slid my rook into place and said 'checkmate,' the kitchen went silent."

Which conclusion best follows from and reflects on this narrative, and why? (A) "Chess is a game played with thirty-two pieces on a board of sixty-four squares." (B) "My brother stared at the board, then grinned and shook my hand. 'About time,' he said, and I realized that all those losses had been teaching me how to win." (C) "Then I went upstairs and did my homework."
items.answer: Conclusion B, because it follows directly from the first-ever checkmate, includes the brother's reaction, and reflects on the meaning of the long string of losses. A is a factual definition unrelated to the story, and C drops the action without reflection.

steps: Identify the arc: years of losses lead to the narrator's first win over the brother who taught him.
A strong conclusion should resolve the moment and reflect on its meaning.
Option A is an encyclopedia-style fact, disconnected from the emotional moment.
Option C simply moves to homework with no reflection.
Option B captures the brother's reaction and reflects that the losses had been lessons; choose B.

items.prompt:
Read this short narrative draft.

"Paragraph 1: The day of the science fair, my volcano model leaked all over the floor before judging even began.
Paragraph 2: My partner, Priya, didn't panic. She grabbed paper towels and a roll of tape and started fixing the base while I held the pieces together.
Paragraph 3: My favorite color is blue, and I have a cat named Pepper who likes to sleep on my backpack.
Paragraph 4: By the time the judges reached our table, the volcano stood firm, and when it erupted on cue, the whole room gasped."

This draft has one paragraph that destroys the story's coherence. Identify the paragraph that does not belong, explain why it breaks the narrative, and say what should happen to it.
items.answer: Paragraph 3 destroys the coherence. It introduces unrelated facts about a favorite color and a cat in the middle of the science-fair crisis, interrupting the event sequence and the focus on fixing the volcano. It should be deleted so the story moves smoothly from the leak to the repair to the successful eruption.

steps: Trace the main event chain: the volcano leaks, Priya and the narrator repair it, the judges arrive, it erupts successfully.
Check each paragraph against that chain for relevance.
Paragraph 3 about a favorite color and a cat has nothing to do with the science fair or the repair.
It interrupts the rising action and breaks the story's unity and flow.
The fix is to delete paragraph 3 so paragraphs 1, 2, and 4 connect logically.
